extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent prosecutors, litigation counsel, judges, and law students/academics interested in double patenting and patent-term issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on identifying, analyzing, and responding to obviousness-type double patenting (ODP) issues within patent families, including the effects of Patent Term Adjustments, terminal disclaimers, and recent Federal Circuit decisions. Focused on prosecution and litigation strategy for related patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type Double Patenting (ODP)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prohibition on issuing a second patent for an obvious variation of an earlier invention; a patent claim is invalid or unpatentable under ODP when the claim is 'patentably indistinct' from a claim in an earlier commonly owned patent or patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ODP is a judicially created doctrine designed to prevent an unjustified timewise extension of the exclusionary right granted by a patent and to prevent harassment by multiple assignees. ODP requires a finding of patentable indistinctness. Courts apply ODP even when the reference is not prior art; the reference may be a claim in an earlier commonly owned patent or application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory double patenting ('same invention')
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory double patenting finds its statutory root in 35 U.S.C. § 101: an inventor may not obtain more than one patent for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory double patenting invalidates a claim when the inventor claims the same invention in two patents or applications. This 'same invention' type is distinct from ODP and is grounded in the statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentably indistinct / indistinctness standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A later claim is not patentably distinct from an earlier claim if the later claim is anticipated by or obvious over the earlier claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indistinctness may be established by anticipation (e.g., genus/species relationships where a genus is anticipated by an earlier species) or by obviousness over the earlier claim. Courts construe claims to determine differences and consider inherent results and admissions. Indistinctness is a threshold requirement for ODP.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODP obviousness analysis differs from §103 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In the ODP context, an obviousness analysis is distinct from an ordinary §103 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ODP courts do not search for a motivation to modify the reference material, nor do they consider objective indicia of non-obviousness. The inquiry is whether the later claim is patentably indistinct from the earlier claim (anticipation or obviousness over the earlier claim), without the §103 requirement to show motivation to combine or secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate references for double patenting need not be prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike §102/§103 references, a double patenting reference need not qualify as 'prior art' and may be a claim in an earlier commonly owned patent or application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections rely on comparison with claims in an issued patent or pending application, not the full disclosure of the reference as with anticipation/obviousness under §§102/103. See MPEP §804.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationale: prevent unjustified extension of patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: ODP is intended to prevent unjustified timewise extension of patent exclusivity when related patents claim patentably indistinct inventions that expire at different times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a later-expiring patent claims indistinct subject matter, the patentee effectively extends the exclusionary right beyond the original patent term, which ODP seeks to prevent. Examples: Vogel (meat vs pork) and the general bedrock principle that when a patent expires the public is free to use the invention and obvious variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationale: prevent harassment by multiple assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: ODP also aims to prevent multiple assignees from filing multiple suits based on patents that claim patentably indistinct variations of the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts view this as a theoretical but real concern; terminal disclaimers promise common ownership to address harassment worries. The doctrine guards against multiple enforcement actions for indistinct claims assigned to different parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer in prosecution to obviate ODP
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer will obviate an ODP rejection during USPTO examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By disclaiming any term beyond the expiration of the earlier-expiring patent, and promising common ownership, an applicant can overcome an ODP rejection. Filing regulations and forms are prescribed by the USPTO (e.g., 37 C.F.R. § 1.321). Terminal disclaimers are routine in prosecution when indistinctness is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer formal requirements (form and common-ownership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 253 and 37 C.F.R. § 1.321(c) a terminal disclaimer must disclaim any term beyond the reference patent's expiration and require that any resultant patent remain commonly owned or become unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The disclaimer must be in prescribed form. It both prevents a timewise extension of term and ties enforceability to common ownership; failing to remain commonly owned can render the disclaimed patent unenforceable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer limitations: cannot cure if reference expired; uncertainty about post-grant curing
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer filed after expiration of the earlier reference cannot cure an existing ODP problem; courts have not uniformly decided whether a post-grant disclaimer can reinstate validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boehringer holds a terminal disclaimer filed after the earlier patent's expiration cannot cure ODP. The Federal Circuit has not decided whether a post-grant terminal disclaimer reinstates validity; litigants face uncertainty and risk of invalidation if they litigate and lose before disclaiming. Filing a post-grant disclaimer may also affect damages and litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant expiration date for ODP includes Patent Term Adjustment (In re Cellect)
rubrics_metrics.description: In re Cellect held that ODP for a patent that has received a PTA must be based on the patent’s expiration date after PTA has been added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When patents within a family receive different PTAs, they can have different expirations despite common priority; ODP analysis uses the PTA-adjusted expiration date, which can render later-expiring family members susceptible to ODP even though default expiration would have been the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between Patent Term Adjustment (PTA) and Patent Term Extension (PTE)
rubrics_metrics.description: PTA (35 U.S.C. § 154(b)(1)) compensates for USPTO prosecution delays and is distinct from PTE under 35 U.S.C. § 156 which compensates for regulatory delays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit treated PTA and PTE as distinct statutory mechanisms for affecting patent term; both can create differences in expiration dates between related patents but arise from different statutory schemes and policy rationales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe harbor for divisional applications (35 U.S.C. § 121)
rubrics_metrics.description: An application that results from an examiner's restriction requirement (a divisional) is protected from being used as a double-patenting reference against patents issuing from either application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants can rely on filing multiple claims in an initial application or use divisional practice to create safe harbor from ODP challenges that would otherwise arise among family members.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR cannot be instituted on ODP grounds; ex parte reexamination can address ODP
rubrics_metrics.description: Inter Partes Review (IPR) institutions are limited to §§102/103 grounds (35 U.S.C. § 311) and thus cannot be instituted on ODP grounds; Ex Parte Reexamination can be based on a substantial new question of patentability including ODP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties raising ODP in post-grant proceedings may need to use reexamination or other USPTO procedures rather than IPRs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court vs USPTO standards for finding ODP in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike examiners, courts may require a showing of an actual timewise extension of patent term or lack of common ownership to find ODP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An examiner can require a terminal disclaimer when there is a risk of extension or harassment; a court may look for concrete harm (e.g., Zimmer — no ODP where patents expired on same day before disclaimer). Litigation posture influences whether a terminal disclaimer is sufficient or whether invalidity will be found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of terminal disclaimers on damages and litigation strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a terminal disclaimer may prospectively disclaim term and thus could reduce available damages or shorten the damages period; courts are split on retroactivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plaintiff considering filing a post-grant disclaimer must weigh losing damages (Georgia-Pacific factors and §286 six-year lookback). Some district courts have allowed full retroactive damages despite a later disclaimer; the Federal Circuit has not settled the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus-species anticipation principle in ODP
rubrics_metrics.description: A later genus claim may be anticipated by an earlier species claim, rendering the genus not patentably distinct from the species in the ODP context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eli Lilly demonstrated that when the earlier species necessarily includes the genus feature (e.g., humans as species of animals), anticipation can establish indistinctness. This is a common resolution path in ODP disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent patricide concept and limits (Allergan ruling)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Patent patricide' describes using a later-filed child patent to invalidate an earlier-filed parent under ODP. The Federal Circuit in Allergan largely rejected patent patricide in the common parent-child scenario.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allergan holds that a first-filed, first-issued, later-expiring claim cannot be invalidated by a later-filed, later-issued, earlier-expiring reference claim having a common priority date. Thus, Cellect's expansion of ODP to include PTA-based expirations does not authorize blanket patricide; the parent/child filing-and-issuance order remains relevant in common situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical prosecutorial responses to In re Cellect and Allergan
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutors must understand that ODP can arise within a portfolio due to PTA differences and adjust prosecution strategy accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible responses include filing terminal disclaimers (often disclaiming later-filed continuations to earlier parents), increasing claim coverage in single applications to rely on divisional safe harbor, and careful management of continuations to avoid creating later-expiring indistinct claims. The market value of added term, particularly in pharma, drives litigation risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODP consequence when earlier reference is expired and challenged patent has PTA
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent has received PTA and a related earlier patent has already expired, an ODP challenge may be unsalvageable because a terminal disclaimer cannot cure when the reference is already expired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Cellect illustrated this situation: patents had expired and could not be terminally disclaimed, so an ODP finding would permanently invalidate the patents. Practitioners should monitor expiration dates and PTA to avoid such outcomes.
